narrative: During the 1950s, Black and African women's hairstyles and hair culture were deeply rooted in their rich heritage and traditions. The afro, a hairstyle created by combing out natural growth of kinky hair, was likely a prominent style during this decade, as it remains an iconic symbol of black identity to this day. Cornrows, a traditional African braiding practice, may have also been popular among women, providing a protective and stylish way to wear their hair. The concept of protective hairstyles, which aimed to reduce breakage and damage caused by environmental factors, was likely understood and practiced during this time. While the source material does not provide specific information about 1950s hairstyles, it is clear that Black and African women's hair culture has a long history of creativity, resilience, and self-expression. As the natural hair movement would later emphasize, textured hair in all its forms - waves, curls, and kinks - was (and remains) a source of pride for many Black and African women.
